identity.title: Lactate dehydrogenase A-dependent redox control of selective mRNA translation directs monocyte fate commitment.

content.abstract: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is a central process that shapes immune responses across diverse contexts, yet how inflammatory cues engage metabolism to instruct monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Here, using a CRISPR-based metabolic screen combined with monocyte-specific perturbations in bacterial lung infection, we identified lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) as a key metabolic regulator of monocyte commitment to the nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)(+) macrophage fate in vivo. LDHA-dependent cytosolic nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD(+)) regeneration enabled selective hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1alpha) translation through its 5' untranslated region (UTR) and is associated with structural remodeling of this region. HIF1alpha then functioned as a downstream effector that promoted the NOS2(+) macrophage fate. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) further acted as an upstream metabolic priming signal that enhanced LDHA-dependent HIF1alpha regulation and supported this differentiation process. Together, these findings suggest that metabolic redox state regulates monocyte fate commitment through selective mRNA translation coupled to RNA structural remodeling.
